h: People like you [more] than you think.
b: After talking with a stranger, people consistently [underestimated] how much the other person liked them. Researchers call it the liking gap.
s: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018), Psychological Science
t: People like you more than you think (the liking gap) #shorts

b: When people were left out of a simple ball tossing game, brain areas linked to the [distress of physical pain] became active.
t: Why rejection feels like physical pain #shorts

b: Strangers who asked each other 36 increasingly personal questions for 45 minutes felt [much closer] than pairs who made small talk.
s: Aron, Melinat, Aron, Vallone & Bator (1997), Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin
t: The 36 questions that make strangers feel close #shorts

b: Couples who did a [novel, exciting] activity together reported higher relationship quality than couples who did something pleasant but familiar.
s: Aron, Norman, Aron, McKenna & Heyman (2000), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
t: What actually keeps a relationship exciting #shorts

h: Watch how they react to your [good news].
b: Partners who answered good news with [real enthusiasm] had stronger, more satisfying relationships. A flat reply did the opposite.
s: Gable, Reis, Impett & Asher (2004), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
t: The good news test every relationship faces #shorts

b: Strangers who looked into each other's eyes for two minutes reported [more affection] for each other than pairs who looked at each other's hands.
s: Kellerman, Lewis & Laird (1989), Journal of Research in Personality
t: What 2 minutes of eye contact did to strangers #shorts

b: In long term studies of couples, [contempt] like eye rolling and mockery was one of the strongest predictors of a breakup.
t: The one sign that predicts a breakup #shorts

h: Your thank you means [more] than you think.
b: People who wrote a gratitude letter [underestimated] how happy it made the person who got it, and overestimated how awkward it would feel.
t: Why you should send that thank you message #shorts

b: People liked strangers more when they believed those strangers [shared their attitudes]. Similarity, not difference, drove attraction.
s: Byrne (1961), Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology
t: Do opposites attract? Psychology says no #shorts

b: Women were most attracted to men when they were [unsure] whether those men liked them back, and they thought about them more.
t: Why mixed signals make you think about them more #shorts
